description: Looking for creative and motivated teammates with skills in Al/ML, coding, UI/UX, data analysis, space science, research, or storytelling. Let's build an innovative solution together!
summary:
"Abandoned but not Forgotten" is an interactive web game built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Players start a journey, choose the Moon, Mars or Deep Space, and scan mystery objects to discover 13 pieces of NASA hardware left behind. These include the Apollo lunar module descent stages, moon buggies, Viking landers, Spirit and Opportunity, Ingenuity, Dawn and Kepler. Each discovery shows a NASA photo, its story and a fun fact. Players earn ranks and finish with a key-facts summary.
It turns silent, retired spacecraft into a story-driven experience for school-age learners. It explains what each explorer was, why it was sent and what it discovered, such as Opportunity's evidence of ancient water on Mars. It covers the hardware in NASA's resource list, and the simple tap-to-explore design works on phones.
These machines changed our understanding of space, yet they are easy to forget. The game makes learning active, builds a personal connection to them and inspires young people to explore science and engineering.
details:
What it does and how it works:

"Abandoned but not Forgotten" is an interactive web game that tells the stories of NASA hardware left behind on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. The player presses Start Journey and chooses a world: the Moon, Mars or Deep Space. They then scan mystery objects to reveal each explorer. Every discovery shows the explorer's name, why it was sent, what it discovered, a real NASA photo and a fun fact. Players earn ranks from Space Cadet to Mission Commander as they find objects, and the journey ends with a summary of important facts. The game has 13 artifacts, including the Apollo lunar module descent stages, moon buggies, ALSEP science stations, Surveyor landers, the Viking landers, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Phoenix and InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and 11, and the Kepler Space Telescope.

Benefits:

Learners explore at their own pace and remember facts through play instead of reading a long list. The information is accurate, written in simple language, and every photo is credited to NASA.

Intended impact:

We want school-age learners and casual space fans to feel a personal connection to robotic explorers that are easy to forget. For example, Opportunity was built to last 90 days and worked for over 14 years. We hope the game inspires curiosity about space, science and engineering.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software:

We built the game with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It runs in any web browser on a phone or laptop, so no special hardware or software is needed to play it. Images come from NASA and are credited in the game. We used an AI assistant (Claude) to help write and refine the code and content.

How it is creative:

Instead of a plain fact sheet, learning is a mission game. Players scan mystery objects, a rover drives across a Mars landscape as they move between worlds, they earn ranks, and each discovery ends with a surprise fun fact. The story of an explorer is revealed one discovery at a time.

Factors our team considered:

Accuracy of the NASA facts, working well on phones, simple language for young learners, clear photo credits, the age group of the players, and a fast, easy-to-use design.
